one_paragraph_summary: In this continuation of his June 3 peace-process column, Panganiban takes up the second of the four Hague Declaration agenda items: socioeconomic reforms -- the 'CASER' -- which Ateneo Law Dean Sedfrey Candelaria (speaking in an FLP lecture) called the acid test of the peace process because 'a just and lasting peace could be reached if the root causes of the armed conflict could be addressed and eliminated.' Formal talks on this topic had stalled since CARHRIHL was signed on March 16, 1998 -- the only of the four agenda items completed -- but were scheduled to resume on June 28 under GRP peace panel head Secretary Jesus Dureza. The column summarizes the communist proposals in five categories: agrarian reform and rural industrialization (expropriate military bases, golf courses, and tourism sites used for agriculture; terminate foreign corporation leases; ban land conversion; prohibit policies allowing agricultural-to-industrial conversion); national industrialization (expropriate US, Japanese, and other foreign monopoly capital; dismantle big compradors and bureaucrat capitalists; support the national bourgeoisie, MSMEs, and a 100% Filipino retail industry); environmental protection (US accountability for former base pollution; domestic processing of minerals); sectoral rights (national minimum wage indexed to cost of living; strike rights in SEZs and public sector; end OFW fees; no LGBTQ discrimination; legalize divorce; free tertiary and vocational education; free healthcare); and international economic relations (reject IMF/World Bank/ADB/WTO dictates; cap foreign equity at 40%; abolish VAT and excise taxes on basic goods; reexamine foreign debt). The column frames these demands without personal endorsement, noting they would require radical changes in the Constitution, laws, policies, and programs -- the 'daunting tasks' facing the GRP negotiators.
